clips.text: Your sweat is an antibiotic. Every drop carries a 47-amino-acid protein that punches holes in E. coli, staph, and even tuberculosis bacteria — and your body makes it without asking, every single day.
clips.image: Extreme macro of human skin with a glowing teal shimmer like an invisible shield, warm skin tones, photorealistic, cinematic light, no text
clips.note: rule 20: aggressive zoom-punch + keyword overlay of the concrete number; 250-400ms pause after claim before re-orientation

clips.text: This is that protein at work — zinc-braced channels drilling straight through a bacterium's membrane.
clips.image: PAYOFF FLASH: reuse twist asset (c7 crop) — zinc-stabilized dermcidin channels perforating a bacterial membrane, deep teal microscopy, no text
clips.note: rule 20: 1.5-2s payoff flash reusing the twist visual; NO new image (reuse c7 asset)

clips.text: In the next nine minutes: the armor you wake up wearing, the workout that turns sweat into artillery, the tiny allies patrolling your skin, and the betrayal that happens every time you shower. But it starts the second you open your eyes.
clips.image: Split triptych feel in one frame: bedroom morning, runner at dawn, shower steam, warm skin tones, photorealistic with teal accents, no text
clips.note: re-orientation: 3-bullet outline + payoff preview; music fades in ONLY after a1's first spoken sentence

clips.text: You wake up and you do not feel armored. You feel groggy, a little sticky, and your first thought is the shower — hot water, soap, the whole reset ritual. But your skin has been standing guard all night.
clips.image: Close-up of brown-haired young man in a blue hoodie waking up in warm morning light, faint teal shimmer on his skin like a garrison glow, photorealistic, no text
clips.note: open loop 1 (mini): tease overlay + push-in

clips.text: The guard is a protein called dermcidin. Only forty-seven amino acids long — tiny, even by protein standards — and your sweat glands manufacture it around the clock.
clips.image: Extreme close-up of forearm skin, beads of sweat glowing faint teal like a line of sentries, deep teal and cyan electron-microscopy style, dark background accents, photorealistic, no text

clips.text: Not when you are sick. Not when you are cut. Always. Your eccrine glands — the ones behind ordinary, everyday sweat — pour it out constitutively. That is the scientists' way of saying the factory never closes.
clips.image: Coiled eccrine sweat gland deep under skin surface, glowing teal, deep teal and cyan electron-microscopy style, dark background, scientific illustration feel, no text

clips.text: And it does not just sit there. Give it salt, give it a little acid, give it a workout — and the armor goes on the attack. That is the stress test.
clips.image: brown-haired young man in a blue hoodie lacing up running shoes at dawn, warm light, determined expression, faint teal glow on skin, photorealistic, no text
clips.note: chapter-end open loop 2: tease overlay + push-in + 1s riser

clips.text: Chapter two: the stress test. You go for a run, and everything your body was quietly doing turns loud.
clips.image: brown-haired young man in a blue hoodie running at dawn through a park, sweat beads catching light with teal glints, warm skin tones, photorealistic, photorealistic, no text

clips.text: Here is the twist nobody expects: dermcidin is lazy in a test tube of clean water. It wakes up inside sweat — in the salt and the slight acidity of a real workout. The conditions you associate with being gross are the conditions that arm the weapon.
clips.image: Extreme macro of a sweat bead on skin, crystalline salt patterns forming inside, teal tint, photorealistic, no text

clips.text: A microbiologist at UC San Diego once called sweat almost like an antibiotic juice. His words, not mine — colorful phrasing, but the chemistry underneath it is real.
clips.image: brown-haired young man in a blue hoodie mid-stride running, slow-motion sweat spray catching golden light, teal shimmer, photorealistic, no text
clips.note: open loop 3 (mini): Gallo quote as color, uncertainty kept (his phrasing)

clips.text: As the water evaporates, the good stuff concentrates. The salt, the acids, the dermcidin — all of it gets stronger as you dry off. Your post-run glow is, chemically speaking, a shield hardening.
clips.image: Macro time-lapse feel: sweat evaporating off skin, teal glow intensifying as water leaves, warm skin tones, photorealistic, photorealistic, no text

clips.text: In the lab, dermcidin kills E. coli, staphylococcus aureus, and a yeast called candida albicans — on contact, no immune system required. A one-protein army.
clips.image: Three types of bacteria under microscope being perforated by glowing channels, teal battlefield, deep teal and cyan electron-microscopy style, dark background, no text

clips.text: But a shield you never see is easy to ignore — until something gets through. Which brings us to the smallest, stupidest injury of your life. The paper cut.
clips.image: Close-up of hand reaching for a sheet of paper, warm tones, a tiny teal spark at the fingertip, photorealistic, no text
clips.note: chapter-end open loop 4: tease overlay + push-in + 1s riser

clips.text: Chapter three: the invasion. A paper cut is nothing — a slit a fraction of a millimeter deep. And yet, the moment it happens, an entire defense grid lights up.
clips.image: Paper edge slicing a fingertip, extreme macro, warm skin tones, photorealistic, dramatic side light, photorealistic, no text

clips.text: Bacteria are everywhere — on the paper, on your skin, in the air itself. The cut is a doorway, and they pour toward it. Most never make it past the lobby. This is the moment the armor earns its name.
clips.image: Bacteria swarming toward a breach in skin, teal battlefield microscopy, deep teal and cyan electron-microscopy style, dark background, no text

clips.text: You feel the sting and reach for a bandage. But before the bandage, something older is already moving: sweat, welling into the wound, carrying dermcidin straight to the breach.
clips.image: brown-haired young man in a blue hoodie wincing, examining a paper cut on his finger, warm indoor light, photorealistic, no text

clips.text: The mechanism has four moves. First: the gland. Coiled deep in your skin, it squeezes dermcidin into the sweat before the drop even surfaces.
clips.image: ONE sweat-gland diagram asset, full view: coiled eccrine gland under skin layers, dermcidin molecules as glowing teal dots flowing upward, deep teal scientific diagram style, dark background, NO text, NO labels, NO letters
clips.note: dataScene beat 1 of 4: staged reveal, one asset; c5-c7 are true crops of this

clips.text: Second: activation. The salt and mild acid of your sweat fold the protein into its working shape. Without them, dermcidin is a key that does not fit the lock.
clips.image: TRUE CROP of the c4 gland asset, zoomed into the activation zone: salt crystals and acidic tint folding a protein ribbon, deep teal, no text
clips.note: dataScene beat 2: true crop of c4 asset

clips.text: Third: the channels. Dermcidin molecules link up into tiny pores — and zinc ions already floating in your sweat lock them rigid, like rivets in a bridge.
clips.image: TRUE CROP of the c4 gland asset, zoomed into channel formation: protein pores with glowing zinc spheres bracing them, deep teal, no text
clips.note: dataScene beat 3: true crop of c4 asset

clips.text: Fourth: the breach. Those rigid channels punch into the bacterial membrane, and the cell leaks to death. This — right here — is the protein from the opening seconds, doing exactly what I promised.
clips.image: TRUE CROP of the c4 gland asset, zoomed into membrane perforation: zinc-braced channels drilling through a bacterium's membrane, the TWIST visual, deep teal microscopy, no text
clips.note: dataScene beat 4 = TWIST; a2 payoff flash reuses this exact asset

clips.text: And it goes further than the usual suspects. In the laboratory, dermcidin even worked against mycobacterium tuberculosis — the bacterium behind TB. In the laboratory. That distinction matters, and I will come back to it.
clips.image: Petri dish with tuberculosis bacteria colonies, a clear zone where dermcidin was applied, teal lab glow, deep teal and cyan electron-microscopy style, dark background, no text
clips.note: uncertainty: TB result is a LAB finding, stated explicitly

clips.text: Your paper cut heals, and you credit the bandage. But the first responder was the sweat you barely noticed — one layer of a front-line defense you wear every single day.
clips.image: Healed fingertip, smooth skin, faint teal shimmer of renewed shield, warm skin tones, photorealistic, photorealistic, no text

clips.text: But dermcidin is not fighting alone. Your skin is a crowded city — and some of the residents are on your side. Meet the allies.
clips.image: Microscopic city of diverse bacteria on skin surface, garrison lights glowing teal, deep teal and cyan electron-microscopy style, dark background, no text
clips.note: chapter-end open loop 5: tease overlay + push-in + 1s riser

clips.text: Chapter four: the allies. About two hundred species of bacteria live on your skin right now. Most are harmless. A few are hired guns.
clips.image: Diverse skin bacteria colony city under microscope, hundreds of species, teal and amber glows, deep teal and cyan electron-microscopy style, dark background, no text

clips.text: One of them is called staphylococcus hominis. It lives in your sweat glands — and it makes its own antibiotic, a chemical weapon aimed with sniper precision at MRSA, the drug-resistant staph that terrifies hospitals.
clips.image: Staphylococcus hominis colony, friendly golden spheres among teal bacteria, deep teal and cyan electron-microscopy style, dark background, no text

clips.text: You did not recruit it. You did not pay it. It just lives there, in the salty dark of your glands, murdering your enemies for rent. Your body outsourced part of its defense to a microbe — and the microbe delivers.
clips.image: brown-haired young man in a blue hoodie smiling, close-up of healthy glowing skin, warm light, teal shimmer, photorealistic, no text

clips.text: Scientists at UC San Diego are turning that discovery into an eczema cream — borrowing the bacterium's weapon to calm inflamed skin. The trials are preliminary. Promising, but preliminary. This is not a pharmacy shelf yet.
clips.image: Laboratory vials and cream research, scientist hands in gloves, teal lab glow, photorealistic, no text
clips.note: uncertainty: eczema cream = preliminary trials, stated explicitly

clips.text: Think about that number again: two hundred species, and evolution has tuned at least one of them to hunt the germ that beats our strongest drugs.
clips.image: Visual comparison: two hundred tiny bacteria silhouettes surrounding one large MRSA invader, teal battlefield, deep teal and cyan electron-microscopy style, dark background, no text

clips.text: So your skin is a garrison: your own protein artillery, plus allied bacteria running patrols. Which raises an uncomfortable question about your daily routine.
clips.image: brown-haired young man in a blue hoodie looking at his own hands thoughtfully, warm bathroom light, photorealistic, no text

clips.text: Because twice a day, you do the one thing that strips the whole garrison away. You step into the shower.
clips.image: Shower running, steam rising, teal shimmer washing down the drain, dramatic, photorealistic, no text
clips.note: chapter-end open loop 6: tease overlay + push-in + 1s riser

clips.text: Chapter five: the betrayal. Hot water, soap, scrubbing — the shower is a siege engine, and your armor is what it is besieging.
clips.image: Shower water blasting across skin, teal armor visibly dissolving, dramatic slow motion, photorealistic, no text

clips.text: Every wash rinses away the dermcidin layer and most of the two hundred species. The garrison does not surrender — it gets evicted. Soap does not distinguish between the invaders and the guards.
clips.image: Dermcidin molecules and bacteria washing away in a drain swirl, teal fading to grey, photorealistic, no text

clips.text: You step out feeling clean, and you are — the smell is gone, the grime is gone. But the shield is gone too, and the rebuild starts immediately.
clips.image: brown-haired young man in a blue hoodie stepping out of the shower with a towel, clean skin, warm bathroom light, photorealistic, no text

clips.text: Here is the good news: within ten minutes of washing, your skin's bacteria start moving back in. Ten minutes — a timeline you can set a watch by.
clips.image: Timeline visual: bacteria repopulating skin minute by minute, 0 to 10 minutes, teal regrowth spreading, deep teal and cyan electron-microscopy style, dark background, no text

clips.text: One honest caveat: not everyone's armor is equal. Dermcidin levels vary from person to person — your shield might be a fortress and mine might be a fence. The science is still mapping why.
clips.image: Split comparison: one person's strong bright teal skin shield versus another's fainter shield, warm skin tones, photorealistic, photorealistic, no text
clips.note: uncertainty: individual variation, stated explicitly

clips.text: So here is the question nobody asks in the pharmacy aisle: if your sweat is medicine — do you really need to shower twice a day? Or are you washing away the armor?
clips.image: brown-haired young man in a blue hoodie staring into a bathroom mirror, question in his eyes, warm light, slow cinematic feel, photorealistic, no text
clips.note: RHETORICAL-QUESTION beat: slower drift + music duck; 1.75s full silence after (gap)

clips.text: Chapter six: the lab. The year is 2001, and a team led by Birgit Schittek publishes a discovery in Nature Immunology: human sweat contains a brand-new antibiotic protein. Forty-seven amino acids. They name it dermcidin.
clips.image: 2001 laboratory, scientist at a bench discovering a glowing protein sample, teal lab glow, photorealistic, no text

clips.text: Forty-seven amino acids — small enough to count, strange enough to matter. Nobody had ever seen a human antibiotic built quite like this one.
clips.image: Protein ribbon of 47 units glowing teal against dark background, deep teal and cyan electron-microscopy style, dark background, scientific visualization, no text

clips.text: Years later, researchers across Edinburgh, Göttingen, Tübingen and Strasbourg cracked its atomic structure — published in PNAS — and found the zinc trick: the channels only hold their shape because zinc ions brace them. Without zinc, the pores collapse like a tent without poles.
clips.image: Scientist at an electron microscope, European lab montage feel, teal accents, photorealistic, no text

clips.text: That is rare in biology — a weapon that needs its battlefield's chemistry to work. Salt to wake it, acid to shape it, zinc to arm it. Your workout is the assembly line.
clips.image: Atomic model of a dermcidin channel, glowing zinc spheres bracing the structure, deep teal and cyan electron-microscopy style, dark background, no text

clips.text: The same PNAS work showed it killing tuberculosis bacteria. Let me be precise, because precision is the point: that happened in a laboratory dish. It is not a treatment. It is not a cure. Sweat does not cure disease — it is one layer of a front-line defense.
clips.image: Tuberculosis bacteria versus dermcidin channels in a lab dish, teal battlefield, deep teal and cyan electron-microscopy style, dark background, no text
clips.note: uncertainty: lab finding, NOT clinical; never claim sweat cures disease

clips.text: You will find blogs claiming dermcidin fights the flu. That claim is unverified — the studies do not show it, so this video will not either. A good shield does not need fairy tales.
clips.image: Person scrolling a phone skeptically, warm light, teal accents, photorealistic, no text
clips.note: uncertainty: flu claim REJECTED explicitly on camera

clips.text: So what do you do with a shield you have been washing down the drain? That is today.
clips.image: brown-haired young man in a blue hoodie walking through a morning city, blue hoodie, warm light, faint teal shimmer on skin, photorealistic, no text
clips.note: chapter-end open loop 7: tease overlay + push-in + 1s riser

clips.text: Chapter seven: today. You do not need to change your life. But you might change one habit.
clips.image: Sunrise over a city, brown-haired young man in a blue hoodie stretching on a balcony, blue hoodie, warm light, photorealistic, no text

clips.text: Remember what sweat is in this story: not a cure, not a miracle — one layer. Soap still matters. Deodorant still matters. Antibiotics still matter. The armor just deserves a vote.
clips.image: Skin cross-section showing defense layers, outermost glowing teal shield, deep teal and cyan electron-microscopy style, dark background with warm skin tones, photorealistic, no text

clips.text: Maybe the second shower becomes a rinse. Maybe the antibacterial soap — the one that nukes all two hundred species — stays in the cabinet on ordinary days.
clips.image: brown-haired young man in a blue hoodie choosing a shorter shower, smiling, warm bathroom light, photorealistic, no text

clips.text: And maybe, on your next run, when the sweat starts, you do not curse it. That is the artillery deploying. Those are the forty-seven amino acids clocking in — the same protein from the first seconds of this video, still on duty.
clips.image: brown-haired young man in a blue hoodie running at sunset, sweat glowing teal in golden light, cinematic, photorealistic, no text

clips.text: If your sweat is medicine — do you still shower twice a day, or do you let the armor stay? Tell us why.
clips.image: brown-haired young man in a blue hoodie looking straight at camera, blue hoodie, warm confident light, photorealistic, no text
clips.note: COMMENT QUESTION: 1.5s VO pause + deeper bed duck after

clips.text: Science note, plainly stated: dermcidin levels vary between people; the tuberculosis and atomic-structure results are laboratory findings, not clinical treatments; the eczema cream is in early trials.
clips.image: Microscopic battlefield panorama, dermcidin channels versus bacteria, deep teal and cyan electron-microscopy style, dark background, no text
clips.note: uncertainty recap, explicit

clips.text: The named studies, so you can check me: Schittek and colleagues, Nature Immunology, 2001; Zachariae and colleagues, PNAS, on the atomic structure; and the UC San Diego team — Gallo and Nakatsuji — on sweat's antibiotic chemistry and the MRSA-hunting bacterium.
clips.image: Lab notebook and petri dishes, teal lab glow, photorealistic, no text
clips.note: rule 24: named studies in VO

clips.text: You have been wearing armor your whole life. You just thought it was sweat.
clips.image: brown-haired young man in a blue hoodie walking away into morning light, blue hoodie, teal shimmer on skin, cinematic wide shot, photorealistic, no text
